report:
Your answer is essentially **no for the general population**: regular vitamin C does **not** meaningfully prevent colds. The strongest evidence is the Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials using ≥0.2 g/day: across 29 comparisons and 11,306 participants, regular vitamin C had no effect on cold incidence in ordinary people; in general-community trials the pooled risk ratio was 0.97 (95% CI 0.94–1.00), i.e. basically no prevention benefit. It concluded routine supplementation is not justified for community use. https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold

NIH’s consumer fact sheet similarly says that for most people, vitamin C supplements do not reduce the risk of getting a cold. https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminC-Consumer/

Important nuance: “doesn’t prevent” is not the same as “does nothing.” Cochrane found regular use modestly shortened colds—about 8% in adults and 14% in children—and a 2023 meta-analysis found about a 15% reduction in severity, while still not showing prevention. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8

There may be an exception for people under brief extreme physical/cold stress—e.g., marathon runners, skiers, soldiers in subarctic conditions—where incidence fell in some trials, but that does not generalize to routine daily use. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/
